newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Big business ventures into Cave of Glowing Skulls.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Big business ventures into Cave of Glowing Skulls.

text.p: When archaeologists crawled into the burial chamber in the Cave of the Glowing Skulls in Honduras, they discovered what they say could be evidence of a hitherto unknown 3,000-year-old civilisation.
They also discovered a new way to pay for a big dig.

Without waiting for a slow-moving government or a university or rich patron to give them a grant, the archaeologists -- plus one former public relations man -- rounded up a posse of commercial sponsors who donated materials and services worth half a million dollars.

Speed was of the essence, according to James Brady, an archaeologist based at George Washington University who worked on the expedition, because ancient sites, no matter how remote, are often looted of their antiquities between the time they are discovered and the time scholars arrive on the scene.

"I will say that while the funding is rather unorthodox, we've probably been able to get more lab analysis than other projects," Brady told Reuters. "The way we've done things has been great for the science."
The chief sponsors of three expeditions to the site, in 1994, 1995 and 1996, were Nissan Motors Corporation, Dole Fresh Foods, Coca Cola of Honduras and others.
GOLDEN ARCHES OUTSIDE CAVE?

Laurence August, a former public relations consultant based in New Orleans, said he put the deal together after a "well-known treasure hunter" backed out. The scientists were initially sceptical, August said by telephone.

"The archaeologists were convinced I was going to put golden arches in front of the cave," he said, referring to the international symbol of the McDonald's fast-food chain. But he said under their agreement the sponsors have the right to a screen credit in any film made of the expeditions and would likely be mentioned in scholarly papers, but they would get little else. "It's prestige," he said of their motivation.

Bob Clucas of Nissan, which provided four vehicles for the project, agreed the main rewards were not financial. "The goal was not to generate advertising publicity," he said by telephone from Los Angeles.

Nissan was satisfied to support a good project, he said. In addition, some of the documentary footage filmed at the remote jungle location might be used in Nissan communications, but Clucas said that had yet to be determined.
GLOWING SKULLS AND SPIDERS

Brady first went to the Cave of the Glowing Skulls -- known locally as Cueva del Rio Talgua -- in 1994, after two U.S. Peace Corps workers and two Hondurans discovered the site and reported it to the Honduran Institute of Anthropology and History, a repository for artifacts.
"That was kind of amazing to begin with," Brady said. "Generally these things aren't reported to the institute, they're looted."

What was even more extraordinary was the burial chamber in the cave: neatly stacked piles of human bones, capped by human skulls, some of them cemented in place in their original positions by calcite-laden water that dripped on them and then hardened into a white coating. The whitened skulls gave the cave its name.

"It was a room-full, except this tunnel was 40 yards (meters) long and on all sides there was bone," Brady recalled. "There were bundles, the flesh had been taken off of them prior to them being taken to the cave ... In many cases, you could see them grouped together exactly where they had been set, you could look it over and read the context."

In the nearby Cave of the Spiders, named for the fist-sized spider-like arachnids inside, the archaeologists found another burial chamber, but this one had been vandalised early on and the scattered bones had been preserved in hardened calcite. The walls were decorated with red and black paint.

Radiocarbon dating of some charcoal found near the entrance to the Cave of the Spiders put the age of both burial chambers at about 915 B.C., Brady said. Further analysis of two bone samples gave a date of approximately 1400 B.C.

Brady said the way the tombs were configured was different from other pre-Colombian civilisations, leading him to believe the Glowing Skulls and Spiders caves may harbour clues to a different group of people living long ago in Honduras.
Artifacts recovered from the caves were turned over to the Honduran historical institute.
